Parts B and C, question Q1: one thread at 8 MiB

Short version. With one thread and an 8 MiB buffer, the new C copy loop was slower than the assembly copy loop in 31 of 32 program runs over 2 test sessions (median per CPU: 1.18 to 2.61 GB/s slower, which is 2.1 to 4.5 %). The agreed decision rule could use only 5 of these 32 runs, and its formal result for the copy question is "not observed". The two rate limits that the rule uses do not fit the data, and the user must decide whether to change them.

H1 (the rate of the old read loop does not depend on the buffer size) gets the word "rejected" by the rule. The measured difference depends on which loop ran directly before. Its absolute value is 3.44 to 5.54 GB/s in one order of the two loops and 0.06 to 0.11 GB/s in the other. The hypothesis table and section B6 give the details.

Words used here

  • CRB: the Arm Phoenix Reference Server (128 cores of the Arm 64-bit instruction set AArch64). All measurements ran there.
  • Plan, handoff: the files plan.md (the reviewed test plan) and handoff.md (the instructions for its execution, with the numeric decision rules).
  • Part A, B, C, D: the parts of the plan. Part A was screening with the existing benchmark. Part B uses the changed benchmark bwx. Part C reads counters of the cores. Part D needs root and was not run.
  • Q1: the first question of the plan: why one thread with an 8 MiB buffer behaves differently from the other buffer sizes. Q1a is about old read, Q1b about copy, Q1c about two rates of one loop. The second question, Q2, is about many threads and has its own page.
  • Kernel, loop: one timed loop of the benchmark. It is not the Linux kernel.
  • bwx: the changed copy of the benchmark bandwidth.c that Parts B and C use. bwx_o0, bwx_o36, bwx_o52 are three more builds for step B3.
  • asm read (asmread): the read loop written in assembly. Per 256 B it runs 8 load instructions and no add.
  • Old read (oldread), old read 2 (oldread2): the C read loop from before 2026-11-13, and a second copy of the same source. oldread@1M is old read on the first 1 MiB of the buffer.
  • New C copy (copy): the C copy loop since 2026-11-13.
  • asm copy (asmcopy), asm copy 2 (asmcopy2): the copy loop written in assembly, and a second copy of the same source.
  • asmcopy_c: step B2: an assembly loop with the machine code of the new C copy loop (same instruction order, same registers q16 to q31), placed at the loop offset of asm copy.
  • asmcopy_c_add: as asmcopy_c, but the two add instructions are placed after the 8 stores, as in asm copy.
  • asmcopy_c_reg: as asmcopy_c, but with the registers q0 to q15, as in asm copy.
  • Loop offset, "modulo 64": the address of the first instruction of a loop, as the remainder after division by 64 B. 64 B is the size of one cache line.
  • -falign-loops=1: an option of the C compiler gcc that stops the compiler from moving a loop start to an aligned address.
  • Process, launch, tag: a process is one start of bwx. It allocates its own buffers. A launch is that start by the run script. The tag of a process is its name in the run script, for example 8M-cpu2-p1.
  • Header line: the line that the run script writes before the output of each process. It has the tag, the load readings and the options.
  • Interval: one timed period of one loop inside a process, here at least 0.3 s. Before the timed period the loop runs once over the buffer without timing (the warm-up pass).
  • Session: one run of all steps. The plan asks for two sessions some hours apart.
  • Rate: bytes moved per second, in GB/s (1 GB = 109 bytes). A copy counts the bytes read plus the bytes written.
  • Median: the middle value of a sorted list. With an even count it is the mean of the two middle values.
  • L1, L2, SLC: the three cache levels of a core. SLC is the system-level cache (L3), shared by all cores. An 8 MiB buffer fits the SLC and does not fit L2. A 1 MiB buffer fits L2.
  • Prefetcher: the part of a core that fetches cache lines before the loop asks for them.
  • Level: asm read at 8 MiB runs at one of two rates: a lower one (about 67 to 69 GB/s in the sweep of 2026-11-02) or a higher one (about 70.5 to 71.7 GB/s). Which one occurs can differ between processes and can change inside a process.
  • Reference interval: an interval of asm read at 8 MiB that is timed directly before or after a compared pair. It shows the level at that time.
  • Low, high, between: the provisional level labels of an asm read interval at 8 MiB: below 69 GB/s, above 70.5 GB/s, or neither. The analysis script prints "changing" for "between".
  • Stable process: a process whose reference intervals all have one label, low or high. Only a stable process gives a value to a decision at 8 MiB.
  • Group: the processes of one size, one variant or one build that are compared together. A level group of a counter table is the intervals of one CPU, one loop and one label.
  • Pair, pair value: two neighbouring intervals of two loops between the same two reference intervals, and the rate of the first loop of "X minus Y" minus the rate of the second.
  • d, e: the two values of one process. d is the median of its pair values of the two compared loops. e is the median of its pair values of the two copies of one loop.
  • A/A control, A/A spread: a loop that exists twice in the program under two names. The A/A spread of a CPU is the largest absolute e of its processes. It shows how much two equal loops differ.
  • Resolved: the plan's word for a difference whose median is larger than the A/A spread and that has one sign in all processes. It needs 3 processes on a CPU, and 2 such CPUs with the same sign. "(-)" and "(+)" give the sign.
  • The five words: "rejected" (the bounded prediction failed in both sessions), "not rejected", "not observed" (an event that the test could have shown did not occur), "not resolved" (the difference is inside the A/A spread), "not tested".
  • Bounded prediction: the one statement of a hypothesis that a step tests, as the plan words it.
  • Description, no decision: values that this page computes for all processes without level labels. They are given next to the rule. They never change a word of the rule.
  • THP, 2 MiB pages, --no-thp: Linux can back memory with pages of 2 MiB instead of 4 KiB (transparent huge pages, THP). With --no-thp the benchmark asks for 4 KiB pages.
  • Huge-page coverage, kB_huge, kB_total: how many kB of the buffer are backed by 2 MiB pages, of how many kB in total. "Full" means all, "none" means 0 kB.
  • thp_collapse_alloc, pgmigrate_success: two counters of /proc/vmstat for the whole system. The first counts huge pages that Linux built from small pages. The second counts pages that Linux moved.
  • Page state: the huge-page coverage of the buffer and the counters of /proc/vmstat, read before an interval.
  • Case (a), case (b): the two outcomes of step B4 that contradict H3a. Case (a): one CPU has at least 10 low and at least 10 high intervals with full coverage. Case (b): the same with no huge page.
  • Counter, PMU: a hardware event counter of a core, read with the Linux call perf_event_open. PMU is the counter unit of the core.
  • l1d_refill, l2d_refill, ll_miss_rd: the event names of the core for a line that is brought into the L1 data cache, into the L2 cache, and for a read that misses the last cache level.
  • Per line: a count divided by the number of 64 B lines that the interval moved.
  • Clock: cycles of the interval divided by the CPU time of the thread in that interval, in GHz.
  • Load, runnable tasks, waited: the Linux 1-minute load average (the average count of tasks that run or wait to run), the count of tasks that can run at one moment, and the time the script waited for at most 2 runnable tasks before a launch.
  • B1: step: new C copy against asm copy with the A/A pair, sizes 4, 8, 16, 32 MiB, CPUs 0, 2, 41, 94, 4 processes each.
  • B2: step: the three variants asmcopy_c, asmcopy_c_add, asmcopy_c_reg against asm copy, at 8 MiB.
  • B3: step: new C copy against asm copy with both loops at offset 0, 36 or 52 modulo 64, at 8 MiB.
  • B4: step: asm read at 8 MiB for 200 intervals with the page state, CPUs 2 and 41, half of the processes with --no-thp.
  • B6: step: old read at 8 MiB and at 1 MiB with reference intervals, CPUs 2, 41, 94.
  • B9: a step for question Q2 that runs 120 threads. It ran directly before B1. This page uses only its end time, for the system load.
  • C1, C2: steps: the schedule of B4 and of B1 at 8 MiB with core counters.
  • D2: step of Part D: the physical addresses of the buffer pages. Not run.
  • H1: hypothesis: old read is limited inside the core at every cache size, and its rate at 8 MiB does not depend on the level of the load-only loop.
  • H2: hypothesis: the low level can change to the high level while the stream runs, and the high level can stay for the next process.
  • H3a: hypothesis: huge-page coverage decides the level. The low level is a buffer that is not fully on 2 MiB pages.
  • H3b: hypothesis: the physical address of the pages decides the level.
  • H4: hypothesis: the copy difference does not come from the kernel code. It comes from something that differs between processes.
  • H5: hypothesis: the copy difference comes from the instruction order of the C loop.
  • H6: hypothesis: the copy difference comes from the address of the loop (36 against 52 modulo 64).
  • est.: an estimate, not a measurement.

Notes to the rows. A note is a limit of the word or a description. It changes no word.

  • H1. The result comes from part 2 only. Part 1 is "not observed": no CPU has stable high processes. The median d per CPU is -2.67 to -1.10 GB/s. It is the median over pairs in two orders. With old read at 8 MiB timed first, directly after an asm read interval, the median pair value per CPU is -5.54 to -3.44 GB/s. With old read at 8 MiB timed second, after old read at 1 MiB, it is -0.11 to -0.06 GB/s. The second value is inside the A/A spread on every CPU (A/A spreads: 0.25 to 1.00 GB/s). The A/A pairs are two old read intervals at 8 MiB, one directly after the other, after an asm read interval. In 384 of 384 such pairs the first interval is slower than the second (median per CPU: -3.79 to -2.71 GB/s). The A/A spread is a median over both orders, so it does not show this difference. Old read at 1 MiB after asm read minus old read at 1 MiB after old read is 0.00 GB/s (median per CPU). So these data do not show that the rate of old read depends on the buffer size. They show that old read at 8 MiB is slower in the interval directly after an asm read interval.
  • H2. The plan gives H2 no bounded prediction in Parts B and C. So no rule gives a word, and the word of rule 11 is "not tested". The second half of H2 (the high level can stay for the next process) has no test here, because each process allocates a new buffer.
  • H3a. Session s1, CPU 2: the low and the high intervals are in different processes. No process has both. Session s2, CPU 41: one process has both the low and the high intervals. CPU 2 has low intervals with full coverage in every session (s1: 200, s2: 400). H3a predicts that every low interval has less than full coverage. The rule of the handoff counts this only together with high intervals.
  • H3b. Part D was not run. No file has the physical addresses of the buffer pages.
  • H4, low intervals. The word depends on the provisional level limits, which are not validated. Stable processes exist only on CPU 2, and all of them are stable low. Description without labels, no decision: d is below 0 in 31 of 32 processes. Description, no decision: the rule for a size without level, applied to all processes at 8 MiB, gives s1 "not resolved" (3 of 4 CPUs resolved), s2 "not resolved" (2 of 4 CPUs resolved). Other sizes, by the rule: 4 MiB: s1 resolved (-), s2 resolved (-). 16 MiB: s1 resolved (-), s2 resolved (-). 32 MiB: s1 resolved (-), s2 resolved (-). H4 predicts 8 MiB only.
  • H5. The word depends on the provisional level limits, which are not validated. Stable processes exist only on CPU 2, and all of them are stable low. Step B1 has no resolved difference at 8 MiB by the rule in sessions s1 and s2. The plan runs step B2 only after a resolved difference in B1. The step was run so that the data exist if the limits are revised. Description without labels, no decision: d is below 0 in 32 of 32 processes.
  • H6. The word depends on the provisional level limits, which are not validated. Stable processes exist only on CPU 2, and all of them are stable low. Step B1 has no resolved difference at 8 MiB by the rule in sessions s1 and s2. The plan runs step B3 only after a resolved difference in B1. The step was run so that the data exist if the limits are revised.

Open for the user.

  • H1. Strict output of the rule: "rejected", because part 2 is resolved in every session. The audit of the words keeps "rejected" and adds the limit that the difference is a position effect. The check of this page proposes "not resolved" under the last paragraph of handoff B.10, because the pair definition does not fit the B6 data: a pair value contains the position difference. The choice between the two words is a judgment. [Ref1][Ref2][Ref19]
  • H3a. Strict output of the analysis script: "not rejected". The handoff gives "rejected" only if one CPU shows a case in both sessions (handoff B.10, deviation A13). No CPU does (session s1: CPU 2, session s2: CPU 41). Reading of the audit of the words: "rejected". Reason: step B4 of the plan has no same-CPU condition ("H3a is rejected if low and high intervals are both observed with full coverage"), and by rule 11 the bounded prediction failed in both sessions. Which wording applies is a judgment. [Ref1][Ref2][Ref19]
  • H3a and the limits. In session s2 every case depends on the provisional limits (see the row above and section B4). If such a case is not counted, that session has no case, and the word is "not rejected" under both readings. [Ref1][Ref2][Ref19]
  • The level limits. Every word that needs a label uses the provisional limits of 69 and 70.5 GB/s. The section on the reference rate describes how they fit the data. This page does not change them.

The hypotheses are quoted in "Words used here". H4 has one row per level label, because the rule decides each label alone [Ref2].

The rows are in the order in which the steps ran. The script reads the runnable tasks twice before a launch: first for launches.txt, then for the header line of the process. So the two values can differ. One of the runnable tasks is the script that reads the value. "Busiest other process" leaves out ps and bash, which are the script itself [Ref22]. A name that starts with kworker or rcu is a thread of the Linux kernel.

Session s1. The 1-minute load average was high at some launches. Its highest value was 90.41 tasks, in step B1. In that step it was 90.41 tasks at the first launch and 0.96 tasks at the last launch. The step before, in folder B9-20261114T012105Z, ran 120 threads of our own benchmark and ended at 2026-11-14T01:23:01Z [Ref20]. Step B1 started at 2026-11-14T01:23:15Z.

Session s1, step B2. The busiest other process is systemd of the account jhan, with 17.8 % of one CPU at one launch. At the other launches of the step no other process is above 0.3 %. The run script runs under the same account, so this is not another user. The tool ps gives the CPU time of a process divided by the time since its start. Hypothesis: this process started seconds before the launch, with the login of our own visit. The start time of the process (ps -o lstart) would confirm or reject it.

Session s2. The 1-minute load average was high at some launches. Its highest value was 116.25 tasks, in step B1. In that step it was 116.25 tasks at the first launch and 1.00 tasks at the last launch. The step before, in folder B9-20261114T043555Z, ran 120 threads of our own benchmark and ended at 2026-11-14T04:37:51Z [Ref21]. Step B1 started at 2026-11-14T04:37:52Z.

The 1-minute load average is an average over about the last minute. So it still counts the threads of a process that has ended. It is therefore no evidence of another user. The evidence of an otherwise idle system is the three readings above: the runnable tasks, the waits and the logged-in users.

Insufficient data: load readings during an interval. The script reads the load only directly before each launch [Ref22]. A reading of the runnable tasks of each account during an interval would give it.

The reference rate and the two level limits

Rule 5 of the plan labels an interval at 8 MiB by its neighbouring reference intervals of asm read: low below 69 GB/s, high above 70.5 GB/s [Ref1]. The handoff then uses a process only if all its reference intervals have one label [Ref2]. The plan calls the two limits provisional. It asks to check them against the new data before they are used [Ref1]. This section is that check. The limits were not changed.

one intervalfirst reference interval of a processbetween the two limits: no label

Session s1

Session s2

Session s1. In 10 of the 25 rows, more than half of the intervals lie between the two limits, where the rule gives no label. Session s2. In 9 of the 25 rows, more than half of the intervals lie between the two limits, where the rule gives no label. Over the 19 rows of B1, B2, B3, B6, C2 (the steps with reference intervals), the median reference rate of a row is between 67.18 and 70.46 GB/s. Over all 25 rows it is between 67.18 and 71.53 GB/s. 25 of the 144 processes with reference intervals are stable at one level. [Ref12][Ref15]

Each row has the reference intervals of all processes of one step on one CPU. For B4 and C1 each interval is its own reference, so the row has all intervals. A row with more than 120 intervals shows every n-th interval, and the numbers at the right count all intervals. The dots are spread vertically so that they do not hide each other.

Open decision for the user. The limits 69 and 70.5 GB/s come from the sweep of 2026-11-02 [Ref1]. The list gives how they fit the reference rates of this page (description, no decision).

  • Session s1. In 8 of the 16 rows of the copy steps (B1, B2, B3, C2) the median reference rate lies between the two limits. These rows are on CPUs 41 and 94. Their medians are 70.19 to 70.41 GB/s. That is 0.09 to 0.31 GB/s below the high limit. In these rows 60 to 93 % of the intervals get no label. In 88 of 120 copy processes at 8 MiB the first reference interval has another label than the median of the later ones. Without the first reference interval, 52 of the 120 processes would have all reference intervals at one level.
  • Session s2. In 8 of the 16 rows of the copy steps (B1, B2, B3, C2) the median reference rate lies between the two limits. These rows are on CPUs 41 and 94. Their medians are 70.12 to 70.46 GB/s. That is 0.04 to 0.38 GB/s below the high limit. In these rows 55 to 92 % of the intervals get no label. In 85 of 120 copy processes at 8 MiB the first reference interval has another label than the median of the later ones. Without the first reference interval, 49 of the 120 processes would have all reference intervals at one level.

The first reference interval is the first timed interval of a new process, and all later ones follow a copy interval. The rule does not leave it out, and this page does not either. This page does not decide whether the limits are revised, or to which values. Until the user decides, every decision that needs a label uses the limits as they are. Each step below also gives a description without labels, marked "description, no decision".

How to read the charts and tables of B1, B2, B3 and B6.

  • One row of a chart is one process. The blue dot is d and the orange diamond is e. The blue number at the left is d. The orange number at the right is e. Both are in GB/s.
  • The shaded band goes from minus to plus the A/A spread of one CPU in one session. The faint blue line marks the median d of that CPU. Each chart has its own axis.
  • In a table, the A/A spread is the largest absolute e of the CPU. "Largest single A/A pair" is the largest absolute difference of one pair of the two copies, before the median of the process is taken.
  • "Order" gives the median pair value with the first loop of "d = X minus Y" timed first, and with it timed second.
  • All columns before the column "Rule" describe all processes of the CPU and decide nothing. The column "Rule" gives the strict result of the decision rule: the number of processes that the rule uses, and its word. A CPU needs 3 processes for a word. A result over the CPUs needs 2 such CPUs with one sign [Ref2].
  • At 8 MiB the rule uses only stable processes. The labels behind "stable" come from the provisional limits, which are not validated. So a word in the column "Rule" at 8 MiB is not a validated decision.

B1: new C copy against asm copy inside one process

Each process times new C copy, asm copy and a second copy of asm copy (asm copy 2) on the same two buffers, with reference intervals of asm read between the pairs [Ref2]. The loop of new C copy starts at 36 modulo 64 and the loop of asm copy at 52 modulo 64, as in the benchmark of 2026-11-13 [Ref23]. The plan asks whether the difference of 2026-11-13 exists inside one process. In that run new C copy was 2.91 % below asm copy at 8 MiB, with the two loops in different processes [Ref1].

B2: three assembly variants of the C copy loop against asm copy

Each variant replaces new C copy in the B1 sequence at 8 MiB. All three variants and asm copy have their loop at 52 modulo 64 [Ref23]. H5 predicts that asmcopy_c, the assembly loop with the instruction order of the C loop, differs from asm copy by a resolved amount of the sign of B1 [Ref1]. The plan runs B2 only after a resolved difference in B1. B2 was run although B1 at 8 MiB is not formally resolved. This is a deviation. Its purpose is that the data exist if the level limits are revised.

B3: new C copy and asm copy with both loops at one offset

Three more builds place the loops of new C copy, asm copy and asm copy 2 at 0, 36 or 52 modulo 64. H6 predicts that the difference between the two loops changes by a resolved amount when both are at one offset [Ref1]. The build bwx_o52 uses the added compiler option -falign-loops=1. Without it gcc moved the C copy loop from offset 52 to offset 0 [Ref23]. B3 was run although B1 at 8 MiB is not formally resolved, for the same reason as B2.

B4: 200 intervals of asm read on one buffer, with the page state

One process maps one 8 MiB buffer and times asm read 200 times. Before every interval it reads the huge-page coverage of the buffer (kB_huge of kB_total) and four counters of /proc/vmstat [Ref2]. Half of the processes ask for 4 KiB pages with --no-thp. Each interval is its own reference: its label comes from its own rate. H3a predicts that every low interval has less than full coverage and every high interval has full coverage [Ref1].

rate of one intervalthp_collapse_alloc rose before the intervalpgmigrate_success rose before the intervalbetween the two limits (69 and 70.5 GB/s)

Session s1

Session s2

Session s1. 4 processes had full huge-page coverage before every interval, and 4 processes had none before every interval. B6: old read at 8 MiB and at 1 MiB, with references

Each process times old read at 8 MiB, old read at 1 MiB (a size that fits L2) and a second copy of old read at 8 MiB, with reference intervals of asm read at 8 MiB between the pairs [Ref2]. H1 predicts two things: the rate of old read at 8 MiB does not differ between low and high intervals, and it does not differ from its rate at 1 MiB [Ref1].

Description, no decision. Session s1. An interval of old read at 8 MiB that follows an asm read interval differs from one that follows an old read interval by -3.79 to -2.79 GB/s (median, per CPU and copy). The largest A/A spread of a CPU is 0.82 GB/s, and the largest single A/A pair is 4.09 GB/s. [Ref9]

One dot is one interval. "After old read" means that the interval before was old read at 8 MiB, its second copy, or old read at 1 MiB. The first interval of a process is not shown, because nothing ran before it.

What this means for part 2. In the B6 sequence one loop of each pair follows a reference interval of asm read, and the other follows an old read interval [Ref2]. So a pair value contains the difference between the two loops and the difference between the two positions.

  • The median d per CPU is -2.67 to -1.10 GB/s. It is the median over pairs in two orders.
  • With old read at 8 MiB timed first, directly after an asm read interval, the median pair value per CPU is -5.54 to -3.44 GB/s.
  • With old read at 8 MiB timed second, after old read at 1 MiB, it is -0.11 to -0.06 GB/s.
  • The second value is inside the A/A spread on every CPU (A/A spreads: 0.25 to 1.00 GB/s).
  • The A/A pairs are two old read intervals at 8 MiB, one directly after the other, after an asm read interval. In 384 of 384 such pairs the first interval is slower than the second (median per CPU: -3.79 to -2.71 GB/s). The A/A spread is a median over both orders, so it does not show this difference.
  • Old read at 1 MiB after asm read minus old read at 1 MiB after old read is 0.00 GB/s (median per CPU).
  • So these data do not show that the rate of old read depends on the buffer size. They show that old read at 8 MiB is slower in the interval directly after an asm read interval.

The position difference is measured. Its cause is a hypothesis: the loop that ran before leaves a state (cache contents or prefetcher state) that changes the rate of old read at 8 MiB in the next 0.3 s interval. A counter run of the B6 sequence, as in Part C, would confirm or reject it: it would show whether the refills per line differ between the two positions. The rule and its result were not changed.

C1 and C2: core counters per 64 B line

The counter runs repeat the schedule of B4 (C1) and of B1 at 8 MiB (C2). Each thread reads five counters of its own core directly before and after every interval. The counters count only the code of the benchmark, not the Linux kernel [Ref2]. A line is 64 B of the bytes that the interval counts. A copy interval counts the bytes read plus the bytes written [Ref3]. The clock is the cycle count divided by the CPU time of the thread. Part C gives a description. The handoff has no decision rule for it [Ref19]. The plan asks C1 for the counts per line at the low and at the high level, and C2 whether the memory-side counts per line differ between the two copy loops [Ref1].

Observation: the count of l1d_refill is lower than the count of l2d_refill in 800 of the 800 asm read intervals of C1 in session s1, 800 of the 800 asm read intervals of C1 in session s2, 160 of the 160 asm read intervals of C2 in session s1, 160 of the 160 asm read intervals of C2 in session s2. A line that enters L2 from the SLC and is then loaded would be expected to enter L1 too. Hypothesis: for this loop the two event names do not count what they say (for example, lines that the prefetcher brings into L1 may not count as L1D refills). Insufficient data to decide it: the event definitions of this core, or a run of the same loop on a buffer that fits L1 and one that fits L2, would show what each event counts. The observation was first made in the short run before session 1, in 970 of 973 counter rows of asm read [Ref24].

Every value is the median over the intervals of the group. The level group of an asm read interval comes from its own rate and the provisional limits. Copy intervals get no level [Ref19]. "LL read miss" is the event ll_miss_rd, a read that misses the last cache level. A value below 0.000001 is printed as "below 10^-6" in a chart and as "below 1 per million" (lines) in a table. The rate panel of a chart prints the number only, because all rates are within a few percent of each other. Every other panel has its own axis from 0 to the value printed under it.

Deviations and decisions that concern this page

  • Level limits. The limits of rule 5 of the plan were not changed. The section on the reference rate gives their strict result and the open decision.
  • B2, B3 and C2 were run although B1 at 8 MiB is not formally resolved. The plan runs them only after a resolved difference in B1 [Ref1].
  • H3a in the analysis script, corrected on 2026-11-14. Before, the script gave each session the result "not observed" when the two sessions had their case on different CPUs. Now the result of a session comes from that session alone. The word over the sessions still needs one CPU with a case in every session (points A13 and A32) [Ref19].
  • H2. The plan gives H2 no bounded prediction in Parts B and C, so its word is "not tested". The level changes that B4 and C1 show are given as a description.

Limits of this page

  • The level limits (69 and 70.5 GB/s) are provisional and are not validated against the reference rates of this page. Every word in the hypothesis table uses them unchanged. A description is not a decision.
  • B1, B2 and B3 have 4 processes per CPU and group. The rule needs 3 stable processes on each of 2 CPUs. No CPU has a stable high process in any step with reference intervals. Stable low processes exist on CPU 2, and 1 on CPU 41 in step B6 of session s2. So under the present limits this design could not give H4, H5 and H6 a word other than "not observed".
  • The first reference interval of a process is the first timed interval after its start. The section on the reference rate gives the number of processes in which it has another label than the later ones.
  • The one-thread steps of the sessions started at 2026-11-14 01:23 and 2026-11-14 04:37 UTC, 3 h 14 min apart. So "two sessions" does not cover a different day or a restart of the machine.
  • The word for H3a depends on the same-CPU condition of the handoff, which step B4 of the plan does not have. The hypothesis table lists this as open for the user.
  • H3b is "not tested". Part D (counters that need root, physical addresses of the pages) was not run [Ref1]. This limit applies to every statement on the cause of the two levels.
  • The vmstat counters count for the whole system. No increase is no proof that the physical pages of the buffer stayed the same [Ref1].
  • A thread that does not run on its CPU for a part of an interval is not flagged in a run without counters. This was found in the short run: one thread of a process with 120 threads had a CPU time of 87.2 % of its elapsed time, and its row has no flag [Ref24]. B1, B2, B3, B4 and B6 ran without counters, so this page cannot exclude such an interval in them. The counter runs C1 and C2 give the CPU time of each interval.
  • The event names of the counters are taken as the core names them. The section on the counters gives one observation that does not fit the names.
  • In step B6 the two loops of a pair are at different positions after the reference interval. Section B6 shows that the position changes the rate of old read at 8 MiB.
  • Insufficient data: the load during an interval. The script reads it only before each launch.
  • The chart colours were not checked with the palette checker of the chart rules. Every chart also uses position, shape or a text label.

The script make_q1_html.py built this page, and test_q1.py tests it [Ref25].
